power-electronics-001.question: When AC is applied to a single-phase bridge rectifier made of four diodes, which of the following correctly describes the path of the current during one half cycle?
choices: All four diodes conduct in parallel and share the current, so each diode carries a quarter of the load current
Only one diode conducts, and the other three carry no current in either half cycle
Two diagonally opposite diodes conduct in series, and the current always flows through the load in the same direction
power-electronics-001.explanation: In a bridge rectifier, the two pairs of diagonally opposite diodes conduct alternately in the positive and negative half cycles of the AC. In both half cycles the current flows through the load in the same direction, so the output has a full-wave rectified waveform. The current always passes through two diodes in series, so silicon diodes drop about 2 × 0.7 V = 1.4 V. A full-wave rectifier with a center-tapped transformer needs only two diodes but requires two secondary windings.
choiceNotes: The four diodes never all conduct in parallel. The conducting pair changes between the positive and negative half cycles.
Only one diode conducting is how a half-wave rectifier works, and no current then flows in the negative half cycle.
Correct. Pairs of two conduct alternately in series, so the forward-voltage drop is also that of two diodes.

power-electronics-002.question: Which of the following correctly describes the output of a three-phase full-wave rectifier that rectifies three-phase AC with a bridge of six diodes?
choices: Its ripple is smaller than with single-phase full-wave rectification, and the ripple frequency is six times the supply frequency
Because there are more phases, its ripple is larger than with single-phase full-wave rectification, so a large smoothing capacitor is always required
The output is not DC but comes out as three-phase AC at the same frequency as the supply
power-electronics-002.explanation: In a three-phase full-wave rectifier, the difference between the highest and the lowest of the three phases (a line voltage) always appears at the output. The output therefore consists of six humps near the peak of the line voltage per cycle, and the ripple frequency is six times the supply frequency (300 Hz for 50 Hz). Because the ripple is small, an output close to DC is obtained even without a large smoothing capacitor, and the circuit is widely used in industrial motor drives and similar equipment. The average output voltage is about 1.35 times the RMS line voltage.
choiceNotes: Correct. Six humps per cycle make the ripple small and its frequency high.
The more phases, the smaller the ripple and the smaller the smoothing capacitor needed.
The diode bridge picks out the difference between the highest and the lowest phase, so the output is a unidirectional voltage (DC).

power-electronics-003.question: A sinusoidal AC voltage of 100 V RMS is full-wave rectified with an ideal diode bridge. Without a smoothing capacitor, which of the following is closest to the average output voltage?
choices: About 90 V
About 141 V
power-electronics-003.explanation: The peak of the sine wave is Vm = √2 × 100 ≈ 141 V. The average of the full-wave rectified waveform is (2/π) × Vm = (2√2/π) × V ≈ 0.90 × 100 ≈ 90 V. 100 V is the RMS value of the full-wave rectified waveform, the same as that of the input. With half-wave rectification the negative half cycles are missing, so the average is half of this, about 45 V.
choiceNotes: Correct. The average is (2√2/π) × 100 ≈ 90 V.
100 V is the RMS value of the full-wave rectified waveform. The average is smaller than the RMS value.
About 141 V is the peak of the sine wave, the value the output approaches with a smoothing capacitor and a very light load.

power-electronics-004.question: Estimate on the assumption that the capacitor supplies all of the load current for one full ripple period. When 50 Hz AC is full-wave rectified, smoothed with a 10,000 µF capacitor, and a constant 2 A flows to the load, which of the following is the approximate peak-to-peak output voltage ripple?
choices: About 1 V
About 2 V
About 4 V
power-electronics-004.explanation: With full-wave rectification the ripple period is half a supply cycle, 1/(2 × 50 Hz) = 10 ms. If the capacitor supplies 2 A during that time, it gives up a charge of 2 A × 10 ms = 20 mC, and the voltage drops by ΔV ≈ I/(2fC) = 20 mC ÷ 10,000 µF = 2 V. In reality the next charging starts slightly before the peak, so the ripple is a little smaller than this estimate. With half-wave rectification the ripple period is 20 ms, giving about 4 V under the same conditions.
choiceNotes: This assumes discharge for only half the ripple period (5 ms). Even with full-wave rectification, the capacitor discharges for almost 10 ms.
This is the value for half-wave rectification. With full-wave rectification the capacitor is charged twice per cycle, so the ripple is half as large.

power-electronics-005.question: In phase control with an AC supply and thyristors, which of the following correctly describes how the average output voltage changes when the firing angle (control angle) α is increased?
choices: The average output voltage stays constant regardless of the firing angle
The larger the firing angle, the higher the average output voltage
The larger the firing angle, the lower the average output voltage
power-electronics-005.explanation: A thyristor starts conducting when a signal is applied to its gate while it is forward biased. Phase control adjusts the part of each half cycle during which current flows by changing the angle α from the zero crossing of the supply voltage to the moment of firing. Increasing α shortens the conduction interval and lowers the average output voltage. The method has long been used in lamp dimmers and in speed control of DC motors.
choiceNotes: Changing the firing angle is precisely how the output is adjusted.
The later the firing, the shorter the interval during which voltage is applied, so the average falls.
Correct. For single-phase full-wave control with a resistive load, the average is proportional to (1 + cos α)/2.

power-electronics-006.question: A 200 V RMS single-phase AC supply feeds a resistive load through a single-phase full-wave rectifier using thyristors, with phase control. Which of the following is closest to the average output voltage at a firing angle of 60°?
choices: About 68 V
About 90 V
About 135 V
power-electronics-006.explanation: With a resistive load the current falls to zero when the supply voltage reaches zero and the thyristor turns off, so the output in each half cycle is the sine wave from α to π. The average is Vd = (2√2/π) × V × (1 + cos α)/2 = 0.90 × 200 × (1 + 0.5)/2 ≈ 135 V. At α = 0 it equals that of diode full-wave rectification, about 180 V. With a strongly inductive load whose current never stops, the average becomes 0.90 × V × cos α ≈ 90 V, so note that the formula depends on the load.
choiceNotes: This is the half-wave phase-control value (√2/π) × V × (1 + cos α)/2 ≈ 68 V.
This is 0.90 × V × cos α, which holds for an inductive load with continuous current. It does not apply to a resistive load.

power-electronics-007.question: In a thyristor phase-control circuit connected to an AC supply, which of the following correctly explains why the thyristor turns off without any action to turn it off from the gate?
choices: The supply voltage reverses every half cycle, and the thyristor turns off naturally when its current falls below the holding current
Removing the gate signal stops the anode current at that instant, and the thyristor stays off until the gate signal is applied again
After a fixed time an internal timer in the thyristor turns it off
power-electronics-007.explanation: Once a thyristor conducts, it keeps conducting even after the gate signal is removed and does not turn off until its current falls below the holding current. In an AC circuit the supply voltage reverses every half cycle and the current falls to zero each time, so the thyristor turns off naturally. This is called line (natural) commutation, and it is why thyristors that cannot be turned off from the gate can still be used for AC phase control. Turning a thyristor off in a DC circuit requires a commutation circuit that applies a reverse voltage, which is why devices that can be turned off from the gate, such as GTOs and IGBTs, later came into use.
choiceNotes: Correct. It relies on the AC current falling to zero, so there is no need to turn it off from the gate.
The thyristor keeps conducting even when the gate signal is removed. Devices such as GTO thyristors can be turned off from the gate.
There is no timer inside a thyristor. It turns off when its current falls below the holding current.

power-electronics-008.question: In a power supply whose input current is not sinusoidal but contains many harmonics, which of the following correctly explains why the power factor is not 1 even if the fundamental of the current is in phase with the voltage?
choices: The harmonic currents are also multiplied by the voltage and greatly increase the active power, so the active power becomes larger than the apparent power
Harmonic currents at frequencies different from the sinusoidal voltage carry no average power, but they increase the RMS current
When harmonic currents flow, the fundamental of the voltage lags the current by 90°
power-electronics-008.explanation: The power factor is the active power divided by the apparent power (RMS voltage × RMS current). The product of a sinusoidal voltage and a harmonic current at a different frequency averages to zero over a cycle, so the active power is determined by the fundamental current alone. The harmonics, however, also increase the RMS current and hence the apparent power, so the power factor becomes the product of the power factor from the phase difference of the fundamental (cos φ) and the ratio of the RMS fundamental current to the total RMS current. For example, with cos φ = 0.9 and a fundamental that is 0.8 times the total current, the power factor is 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72. The input current of a rectifier with capacitor smoothing is such a case, and power factor correction circuits bring the current closer to a sine wave.
choiceNotes: Active power never exceeds apparent power. The power factor lies between 0 and 1.
Correct. Only the RMS current increases, not the active power, so the power factor falls.
Harmonic currents do not shift the phase of the voltage. The power factor falls because the RMS current increases.

power-electronics-009.question: In a step-down chopper (buck converter), which of the following correctly describes the path of the inductor current while the switch is off?
choices: It keeps flowing from the input supply through the switch into the inductor
It freewheels through the diode and keeps flowing from the inductor to the output
The inductor current drops to zero the instant the switch turns off and flows nowhere
power-electronics-009.explanation: In a buck converter, while the switch is on, current flows from the input through the inductor to the output and energy is stored in the inductor. When the switch turns off, the inductor tries to keep its current flowing, so the diode (freewheeling diode) conducts and current flows from ground through the diode and the inductor to the output. The current on the output side is therefore uninterrupted, which keeps the output ripple small. Replacing this diode with a MOSFET is synchronous rectification.
choiceNotes: While the switch is off, no current flows from the input supply. The input current of a buck converter is pulsating.
Correct. The inductor current keeps flowing along the path through the diode.
The inductor current cannot change abruptly. Trying to stop it suddenly produces a high voltage.

power-electronics-010.question: For an ideal step-up chopper (boost converter) with an input voltage of 5 V and a switch duty cycle of 0.6, which of the following is the output voltage in continuous conduction mode?
choices: 3 V
8 V
power-electronics-010.explanation: The output voltage of an ideal boost converter is Vout = Vin/(1 − D). 5 V ÷ (1 − 0.6) = 5 ÷ 0.4 = 12.5 V. The formula follows from the balance of volt-seconds across the inductor, with Vin applied while the switch is on and (Vout − Vin) while it is off: Vin × D = (Vout − Vin) × (1 − D). The 3 V of D × Vin is the formula of the buck converter.
choiceNotes: This is D × Vin, the buck-converter formula. The output of a boost converter is higher than its input.
This is (1 + D) × Vin, which is not the boost-converter formula.

power-electronics-011.question: For an ideal buck-boost chopper (inverting buck-boost converter) with an input voltage of 12 V and a duty cycle of 0.6, which of the following is the magnitude of the output voltage in continuous conduction mode?
power-electronics-011.explanation: In an inverting buck-boost converter, energy from the input is stored in the inductor while the switch is on and released to the output through the diode while it is off. From the volt-second balance of the inductor, Vin × D = Vout × (1 − D), the magnitude of the output voltage is Vout = Vin × D/(1 − D) = 12 × 0.6/0.4 = 18 V. The output polarity is opposite to that of the input (negative with respect to ground). It works as a step-down converter for D < 0.5 and a step-up converter for D > 0.5, and at D = 0.5 the output magnitude equals the input.
choiceNotes: This is D × Vin, the buck-converter formula.
Correct. 12 × 0.6 ÷ 0.4 = 18 V, with the polarity opposite to the input.
This is Vin/(1 − D), the boost-converter formula.

power-electronics-012.question: Which of the following is the correct basis for deriving the ideal output voltage Vout = D × Vin of a buck converter?
choices: In steady state the inductor current returns to its starting value every period, so the voltage across the inductor averages to zero over a period
In steady state the output capacitor current is always zero, so the capacitor voltage stays constant regardless of whether the switch is on or off
While the switch is on no voltage appears across the inductor, so the output voltage equals the input voltage
power-electronics-012.explanation: The change in inductor current is determined by the time integral of the voltage across it (V = L di/dt). In steady state the current returns to the same value every period, so the voltage across the inductor averages to zero over a period (volt-second balance). In a buck converter, (Vin − Vout) appears while the switch is on and −Vout while it is off, so (Vin − Vout) × D = Vout × (1 − D) gives Vout = D × Vin. The conversion ratios of boost and buck-boost converters are obtained in the same way.
choiceNotes: Correct. The conversion ratio comes from volt-second balance.
The capacitor current only averages to zero over a period; it is not always zero. The ripple current flows into the capacitor and becomes the output voltage ripple.
While the switch is on, (Vin − Vout) appears across the inductor and its current rises.

power-electronics-013.question: For an ideal buck converter with an input voltage of 12 V, an output voltage of 3 V, an inductance of 15 µH and a switching frequency of 300 kHz, which of the following is the peak-to-peak inductor ripple current in continuous conduction mode?
choices: 2 A
power-electronics-013.explanation: The duty cycle is D = 3/12 = 0.25, so the on-time is D/f ≈ 0.833 µs. During the on-time 12 − 3 = 9 V appears across the inductor, so the current rises by ΔI = (Vin − Vout) × D/(L × f) = 9 × 0.25/(15 µH × 300 kHz) = 2.25/4.5 = 0.5 A. During the off-time it falls by Vout × (1 − D)/(L × f) = 3 × 0.75/4.5 = 0.5 A, confirming that it returns to its starting value every period. Doubling either the inductance or the frequency halves the ripple.
choiceNotes: This is half the ripple (the swing from the average).
This forgets to multiply by the duty cycle D. The 9 V appears only during the on-time.

power-electronics-014.question: Which of the following correctly describes continuous conduction mode (CCM) of a DC-DC converter?
choices: Operation in which a DC current of constant magnitude flows from the input supply at all times, regardless of the state of the switch
Operation in which the switch stays on all the time and current keeps flowing
Operation in which the inductor current keeps flowing and never falls to zero during a period
power-electronics-014.explanation: In continuous conduction mode the inductor current ripples but never falls to zero within a period. When the load current decreases, the valleys of the current reach zero and stay there for a while, and the converter moves into discontinuous conduction mode (DCM). Formulas such as Vout = D × Vin for the buck converter and Vout = Vin/(1 − D) for the boost converter hold in continuous conduction mode. In discontinuous conduction mode the output voltage also depends on the load current.
choiceNotes: In a buck converter the input current is pulsating, flowing only while the switch is on. The modes are distinguished by the inductor current.
The switch turns on and off periodically. A switch that stays on cannot convert the voltage.
Correct. The condition for continuous conduction mode is that the inductor current never falls to zero.

power-electronics-015.question: In an ideal buck converter (freewheeling through a diode) with an input voltage of 12 V, an output voltage of 3 V, an inductance of 15 µH and a switching frequency of 300 kHz, the load current is gradually reduced. Which of the following is the minimum output current that keeps continuous conduction mode (the boundary with discontinuous conduction mode)?
choices: 1 A
power-electronics-015.explanation: The inductor current is a triangular wave around its average (the output current) with a peak-to-peak ripple of ΔI = 9 × 0.25/(15 µH × 300 kHz) = 0.5 A. Its valley is "output current − ΔI/2", so when the output current falls below ΔI/2 = 0.25 A, the valley reaches zero and the converter enters discontinuous conduction mode. For the 3 V output this happens when the load resistance exceeds 12 Ω (a lighter load). In a synchronous buck converter the inductor current can also flow in the negative direction, so it can keep operating in continuous conduction mode even at light load.
choiceNotes: Correct. The boundary is half the ripple, ΔI/2 = 0.25 A.
This is the ripple itself, twice the boundary value.
This is half of the 2 A ripple obtained when the duty cycle is forgotten.

power-electronics-016.question: Assume that the entire AC component of the inductor ripple current (0.6 A peak to peak) flows into the output capacitor of a buck converter. With a switching frequency of 300 kHz and an output capacitance of 25 µF (ignore the ESR), which of the following is the peak-to-peak output voltage ripple?
choices: 10 mV
40 mV
80 mV
power-electronics-016.explanation: The current into the capacitor is a triangular wave with an amplitude of ΔI/2. The charge that enters the capacitor during the half period T/2 when this current is positive is the area of a triangle, (1/2) × (T/2) × (ΔI/2) = ΔI × T/8. The voltage ripple is therefore ΔV = ΔI/(8fC) = 0.6/(8 × 300 kHz × 25 µF) = 10 mV. In a real capacitor the voltage ΔI × ESR from the ESR is added, which is why ceramic capacitors with low ESR are often used.
choiceNotes: This is ΔI/(2fC), which greatly overestimates the charge carried by the triangular current.
This is ΔI/(fC), which assumes the ripple current flows in the same direction for a whole period.

power-electronics-017.question: In a DC-DC converter with a low output voltage, which of the following is the main purpose of synchronous rectification, which uses a MOSFET in place of the freewheeling diode?
choices: To make the output voltage higher than the input voltage
To keep the switching frequency constant automatically even when the load current changes
To reduce the conduction loss caused by the diode forward voltage and raise efficiency
power-electronics-017.explanation: A diode has a forward voltage of about 0.3 to 0.5 V even if it is a Schottky barrier diode, producing a loss of current × forward voltage. Turning on a MOSFET with a low on-resistance in place of the diode changes the loss to current² × on-resistance, which can reduce it greatly. The lower the output voltage, such as around 1 V, the larger the diode drop relative to the output, so synchronous rectification helps more. In exchange, the switches must be driven with a dead time so that the two are never on at the same time.
choiceNotes: Whether the converter steps up depends on the circuit topology, not on synchronous rectification.
The switching frequency is set by the control circuit and has nothing to do with synchronous rectification.
Correct. It replaces the loss from the forward voltage with the small loss from the MOSFET on-resistance.

power-electronics-018.question: In a synchronous buck converter, which of the following correctly describes the path of the inductor current during the dead time when both the upper and lower MOSFETs are off?
choices: The inductor current stops completely, but only during the dead time
It flows through the body diode of the lower MOSFET (or a Schottky barrier diode in parallel with it)
It passes through the gate insulator of the upper MOSFET and flows back from the gate-driver supply to the input supply
power-electronics-018.explanation: The inductor current cannot stop abruptly, so while both MOSFETs are off, the body diode of the lower MOSFET conducts and keeps the current flowing. The body diode has a large forward voltage and a long reverse recovery time, so too long a dead time increases losses. Too short a dead time, on the other hand, lets the upper and lower MOSFETs be on together, and a shoot-through current short-circuits the input. The dead time is therefore kept to the minimum the devices allow, and a Schottky barrier diode with a low forward voltage is sometimes placed in parallel.
choiceNotes: Trying to stop the inductor current abruptly produces a high voltage. The current keeps flowing through another path.
Correct. During the dead time the body diode takes over the current.
The gate is insulated and is not a path for the main current.

power-electronics-019.question: Assume that the power lost during a transition is, on average, half of voltage × current. For a power device switching 400 V and 10 A with turn-on and turn-off transition times of 50 ns each and a switching frequency of 100 kHz, which of the following is closest to the switching loss?
power-electronics-019.explanation: The energy lost in one transition is (1/2) × V × I × t, so turn-on and turn-off together lose (1/2) × 400 × 10 × (50 + 50) ns = 200 µJ per period. Multiplying by the number of periods per second (100 kHz) gives a switching loss of 200 µJ × 100,000 = 20 W. Switching loss is proportional to frequency, so at 200 kHz it rises to 40 W. SiC and GaN devices, which switch faster, and soft switching are ways to reduce this loss.
choiceNotes: This counts only one of the two transitions. Each period has both a turn-on and a turn-off.
This uses V × I instead of V × I/2 for the power during the transition.

power-electronics-020.question: In a DC-DC converter, which of the following correctly combines the main reason efficiency drops sharply at very small load currents with a countermeasure?
choices: The lighter the load, the larger the conduction loss, in proportion to the square of the current, so the switch is replaced by one with a higher on-resistance to limit the current
At light load the inductor ripple current becomes zero and the control loop stops, so the inductance is reduced to increase the ripple and keep the control running
Losses that do not depend on current, such as gate driving, become a larger share, so the converter switches to PFM or burst mode to reduce the number of switching events
power-electronics-020.explanation: Conduction loss is proportional to the square of the current, so it becomes small at light load. The losses for charging and discharging the gates, part of the switching losses and the supply current of the control circuit, however, stay roughly constant regardless of the load current, so they pull efficiency down sharply when the output power is small. At light load the converter therefore switches to PFM (pulse-frequency modulation), which lowers the frequency, or burst mode, which switches for several periods and then rests, to reduce the number of switching events. In exchange, the ripple frequency changes and the ripple tends to grow.
choiceNotes: Conduction loss actually becomes smaller at light load. What stands out at light load are the losses that do not depend on current.
Reducing the inductance does not raise efficiency. More ripple actually increases losses.
Correct. The number of switching events is reduced to cut the losses that do not depend on current.

power-electronics-021.question: In a power supply that makes DC from the AC mains, which of the following is the main reason isolated converters, which isolate input from output with a transformer, are used?
choices: To separate input and output electrically to prevent electric shock, and to obtain large voltage ratios from the turns ratio
Because a transformer alone, without any switching, can convert a DC voltage directly into a DC voltage of a different magnitude
Because inserting a transformer always reduces the switching loss to zero
power-electronics-021.explanation: In a power supply connected to the AC mains, electrically isolating the output side, which people may touch, from the input side is a basic safety requirement. An isolated converter applies a voltage switched at high frequency to a small transformer and rectifies its output into DC. The turns ratio of the transformer makes large step-down ratios, such as from several hundred volts to 5 V, possible without extreme duty cycles. Typical topologies include the flyback converter for low power, and the forward converter and full-bridge converter for higher power.
choiceNotes: Correct. Isolation for safety and large conversion ratios from the turns ratio are the main reasons.
A transformer cannot convert DC. The voltage is first turned into AC by switching and then applied to the transformer.
Inserting a transformer does not eliminate switching loss.

power-electronics-022.question: Which of the following correctly describes the operation of a flyback converter?
choices: While the switch is on, energy is sent directly from the input to the output through the transformer, and while it is off, the secondary diode is reverse biased and nothing happens
While the switch is on, energy is stored in the transformer (a coupled inductor), and while it is off, it is released to the output through the secondary diode
It converts the voltage with only a mains-frequency transformer and diodes, without any switch
power-electronics-022.explanation: The transformer of a flyback converter works as an inductor with coupled primary and secondary windings. While the switch is on, the secondary diode is reverse biased, the primary current rises and magnetic energy is stored. When the switch turns off, the winding voltages reverse, the diode conducts and the stored energy is released to the output. With few parts it is widely used in small power supplies up to about 100 W, such as AC adapters, but the surge caused by the leakage inductance of the transformer must be suppressed with a snubber circuit.
choiceNotes: Sending energy directly to the output while the switch is on is how a forward converter operates.
Correct. Like a buck-boost converter, it stores energy and then releases it.
A flyback converter switches at high frequency.

power-electronics-023.question: In a forward converter, which of the following correctly explains why a transformer reset winding (or a clamp circuit) is needed?
choices: To switch the transformer turns ratio automatically and lower the output voltage when the secondary current becomes too large, protecting the diodes and switch from overcurrent
To return the magnetizing energy stored in the core while the switch is on during the off-time, resetting the flux and preventing core saturation
To keep a DC current flowing in the primary of the transformer so that the core stays magnetized in one direction
power-electronics-023.explanation: A forward converter delivers power to the output through the transformer while the switch is on, and its output side has the same form as a buck converter with an inductor. While the switch is on, voltage stays applied to the primary winding, so the magnetizing current and the core flux keep increasing. Unless this flux is reset every period, it accumulates, the core saturates and a large current flows. With a reset winding of the same number of turns as the primary, the reset takes as long as the on-time, so the duty cycle is limited to 0.5 or less.
choiceNotes: A reset winding is not for switching the turns ratio.
Correct. The flux is reset every period to prevent core saturation.
Magnetizing the core in one direction with DC makes it saturate more easily, which is counterproductive.

power-electronics-024.question: In sinusoidal PWM for an inverter, which of the following correctly describes how the switches are turned on and off?
choices: The switches change state only once per half cycle of the desired output frequency
Without a carrier, the on and off states of the switches are chosen at random so that the average of many pulses approaches a sine wave
The desired sine wave (reference) is compared with a triangular wave (carrier), and the upper switch is on while the reference is larger
power-electronics-024.explanation: Sinusoidal PWM compares a sine-wave reference at the desired output frequency with a triangular carrier of much higher frequency. Turning on the upper switch while the reference is larger than the carrier and the lower switch while it is smaller gives a voltage whose pulse widths follow the sine wave. When this voltage is smoothed, for example by the inductance of the motor windings, a sinusoidal component proportional to the reference remains. Switching only once per half cycle is called a square-wave inverter, whose output contains many low-order harmonics.
choiceNotes: This is how a square-wave inverter works, and its output contains many low-order harmonics such as the 5th and 7th.
Random switching cannot control the magnitude and frequency of the output sine wave accurately.
Correct. Comparing the reference with the carrier makes the pulse widths follow the sine wave.

power-electronics-025.question: For inverters that make single-phase AC from a DC voltage E, which of the following correctly compares the output voltage of a half bridge (two switches) and a full bridge (four switches)?
choices: The half-bridge output swings between +E/2 and −E/2 and the full-bridge output between +E and −E, so the output voltage can be doubled
With twice as many switches, the full bridge only has more loss, and the output voltage it can deliver is exactly the same as that of the half bridge
A half bridge can output only a unidirectional DC voltage, so a full bridge is needed to apply an AC voltage to a load
power-electronics-025.explanation: In a half bridge the load is connected between the midpoint of the DC supply, split by two capacitors, and the junction of the two switches, so the load sees either +E/2 or −E/2. In a full bridge the load is connected between the junctions of two legs, so besides +E and −E it can also output 0 by connecting both ends to the same side. The same DC voltage gives twice the output voltage, and the three levels can also be used to reduce PWM harmonics. A three-phase inverter is built from three legs (six switches).
choiceNotes: Correct. A full bridge outputs the difference between two legs, so the output voltage is doubled.
For the same DC voltage, the output voltage of a full bridge is twice that of a half bridge.
A half bridge can also output AC by turning its two switches on alternately.

power-electronics-026.question: An inverter leg on a 600 V DC supply is operated with sinusoidal PWM at a modulation index of 0.8. Which of the following is the amplitude (peak) of the fundamental of the leg output voltage with respect to the midpoint of the DC supply?
power-electronics-026.explanation: The modulation index m is the reference amplitude divided by the carrier amplitude. In the linear range with m of 1 or less, the amplitude of the fundamental of the leg output voltage is m × E/2, which here is 0.8 × 600/2 = 240 V. At m = 1 it reaches its maximum of 300 V (E/2), and a higher voltage cannot be produced while staying with sinusoidal PWM. Changing the modulation index adjusts the magnitude of the AC output voltage without changing the DC voltage.
choiceNotes: This is E/2, the maximum at a modulation index of 1.
This multiplies E rather than E/2 by the modulation index. The leg output swings between ±E/2 about the midpoint.

power-electronics-027.question: A three-phase inverter on a 400 V DC supply is operated with sinusoidal PWM at a modulation index of 1. Which of the following is closest to the RMS value of the fundamental of the output line-to-line voltage?
choices: About 141 V
About 245 V
About 283 V
power-electronics-027.explanation: The fundamental of each phase leg output has an amplitude of m × E/2 = 200 V, whose RMS value is 200/√2 ≈ 141 V (the phase voltage). The line voltage is the difference between two phases, with a magnitude √3 times the phase voltage, so its RMS value is √3 × 141 ≈ 245 V, that is, (√3/(2√2)) × m × E ≈ 0.612 × 400 ≈ 245 V. To extend this limit slightly, adding a third harmonic to the three-phase references and space vector modulation are often used.
choiceNotes: This is the RMS phase voltage (voltage with respect to the midpoint). The line voltage is √3 times larger.
This is the DC voltage divided by √2, which is not the formula for the line voltage with sinusoidal PWM.

power-electronics-028.question: In a sinusoidal PWM inverter, which of the following correctly describes what happens when the modulation index is made larger than 1 (overmodulation)?
choices: The fundamental of the output voltage keeps increasing in proportion to the modulation index, and because there are more pulses, low-order harmonics actually decrease
The output voltage of the inverter becomes zero and a protection function stops the inverter
Pulses are dropped where the reference exceeds the carrier range, so the fundamental no longer increases proportionally and low-order harmonics increase
power-electronics-028.explanation: When the modulation index exceeds 1, near the peaks of the reference the reference stays above the carrier all the time, so the switches stop changing state there and pulses are dropped. The fundamental therefore no longer increases in proportion to the modulation index, and low-order harmonics such as the 5th and 7th increase. The limit as the modulation index grows is a square wave, whose fundamental amplitude is at most (4/π) × E/2 ≈ 1.27 × E/2. In the high-speed range, where as much output voltage as possible is wanted, overmodulation is sometimes used despite the added distortion.
choiceNotes: Beyond a modulation index of 1, the fundamental no longer increases proportionally and low-order harmonics increase.
The output does not become zero; it approaches a square wave instead.
Correct. The linear relationship breaks down and the output approaches a square wave.

power-electronics-029.question: In a PWM inverter driving a motor, which of the following correctly describes the effect of raising the carrier frequency?
choices: The current ripple becomes smaller and audible noise is easier to reduce, but switching loss increases roughly in proportion to the frequency
Finer switching actually reduces the switching loss, but the motor current ripple becomes larger and the noise also increases
The frequency of the fundamental of the inverter output rises in proportion to the carrier frequency, so the motor turns correspondingly faster
power-electronics-029.explanation: Raising the carrier frequency moves the harmonic components produced by PWM to higher frequencies, where the inductance of the motor windings smooths them more easily, so the current ripple becomes smaller. Raising the carrier above the range audible to the human ear (up to about 20 kHz) also makes the motor quieter. On the other hand, the switches change state more often, so the switching loss increases roughly in proportion to the frequency. The motor speed is set by the frequency of the reference, not by the carrier frequency.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is a choice between current quality and switching loss.
More switching events increase the switching loss. The current ripple becomes smaller.
The fundamental frequency of the output is set by the reference. Changing the carrier frequency does not change the speed.

power-electronics-030.question: In a voltage-source PWM inverter, which of the following correctly describes the effect of the dead time on the output voltage?
choices: During the dead time the output terminal is connected to nothing and the output voltage is always zero, so the output voltage drops by a fixed fraction regardless of the current direction
The dead time only prevents shoot-through of the upper and lower switches; it does not affect the output voltage and merely adds a little loss
The output voltage during the dead time is set by the current direction, causing a voltage error that depends on the direction and distorting the current at low output voltages
power-electronics-030.explanation: During the dead time both the upper and lower switches are off, so the voltage of the output terminal is determined by whichever diode carries the current. If the current flows out to the load, the lower diode conducts and the output goes to the negative side; if it flows in, the upper diode conducts and the output goes to the positive side. An error that makes the voltage slightly lower (or higher) than the command therefore arises according to the current direction, and the waveform is distorted near the zero crossings of the current. The effect is most visible at low speed, where the output voltage is small, so dead-time compensation, which corrects the command according to the current direction, is used.
choiceNotes: The voltage is not necessarily zero; whether it goes to the positive or negative side depends on the current direction.
The dead time causes an error in the output voltage, with a large effect especially at low voltages.
Correct. The sign of the error changes with the current direction, so the current is distorted.

power-electronics-031.question: The gate drive voltage is 10 V, and currents other than the gate charge are ignored. When a high-side MOSFET with a gate charge of 100 nC is driven by a bootstrap circuit, which of the following is the minimum capacitance that keeps the drop in the bootstrap capacitor voltage at one turn-on to 0.5 V or less?
choices: 10 nF
50 nF
200 nF
power-electronics-031.explanation: When the MOSFET turns on, the bootstrap capacitor gives the gate a charge Qg, and its voltage drops by ΔV = Qg/C. Keeping ΔV ≤ 0.5 V requires C ≥ Qg/ΔV = 100 nC ÷ 0.5 V = 200 nF. In practice about ten times this value (about 2 µF) is often chosen, allowing for the current drawn by the gate-drive circuit, leakage currents and component tolerances. The capacitor is charged while the lower switch is on, so the circuit is not suited to applications that keep the upper switch on for a long time.
choiceNotes: This divides the charge by the 10 V drive voltage, giving a capacitance whose voltage would fall all the way to zero.
This multiplies the charge by the voltage drop, and the units do not even match.
Correct. 100 nC ÷ 0.5 V = 200 nF.

power-electronics-032.question: In a boost-type power factor correction circuit (PFC circuit) for a power supply that works from 100 to 240 V AC, which of the following correctly explains why the DC output voltage is often set to about 380 to 400 V?
choices: The higher the DC output voltage is set, the more the power factor rises above 1, so the input current can be reduced further
A boost converter can only output a voltage higher than its input, so the output must exceed the peak input voltage (about 339 V for 240 V RMS)
The PFC circuit is a buck converter, so the DC output voltage is kept below the peak input voltage to protect the downstream isolated converter and smoothing capacitor from overvoltage
power-electronics-032.explanation: A boost-type power factor correction circuit takes the rectified, pulsating voltage as its input and controls the switch so that the input current becomes a sine wave of the same shape as the voltage. A boost converter cannot output a voltage lower than its input, so the DC output voltage must always be higher than the peak input voltage. The peak of 240 V RMS is √2 × 240 ≈ 339 V, so the output is set to about 380 to 400 V with some margin. A downstream isolated DC-DC converter then turns this DC voltage into the voltages required.
choiceNotes: The power factor never exceeds 1.
Correct. The output of a boost converter must be higher than the peak input.
A typical power factor correction circuit is a boost converter and outputs a voltage higher than the peak input.

power-electronics-033.question: Which of the following is the synchronous speed of a four-pole induction motor operated from three-phase AC at 50 Hz?
choices: 750 min⁻¹
1500 min⁻¹
3000 min⁻¹
power-electronics-033.explanation: The synchronous speed is the speed of the rotating magnetic field created by the three-phase stator windings, given by n_s = 120f/p [min⁻¹] (f: frequency, p: number of poles). At 50 Hz with four poles it is 120 × 50/4 = 1500 min⁻¹. In regions with 60 Hz, the same motor has a synchronous speed of 1800 min⁻¹. The rotor of an induction motor turns slightly slower than the synchronous speed.
choiceNotes: This puts the 4 poles into 60f/p as if they were pole pairs.
Correct. 120 × 50 ÷ 4 = 1500 min⁻¹.
This is the synchronous speed of a two-pole motor. With four poles the field takes two supply cycles to make one revolution.

power-electronics-034.question: A four-pole induction motor operating at 60 Hz is running with a slip of 0.05. Which of the following is the rotor speed?
choices: 1710 min⁻¹
1800 min⁻¹
1890 min⁻¹
power-electronics-034.explanation: The synchronous speed is 120 × 60/4 = 1800 min⁻¹. The slip is s = (n_s − n)/n_s, so the rotor speed is n = n_s × (1 − s) = 1800 × 0.95 = 1710 min⁻¹. The rate at which the rotor conductors cut the rotating field is proportional to the difference from the synchronous speed, so the frequency of the rotor current is s × f = 0.05 × 60 = 3 Hz. The rated slip of a typical induction motor is a few percent.
choiceNotes: This is the synchronous speed. An induction motor turns slower than the synchronous speed.
This adds the slip to the synchronous speed. When running as a motor, it turns slower than the synchronous speed.

power-electronics-035.question: Which of the following correctly explains why an induction motor cannot run at exactly the synchronous speed while operating as a motor?
choices: Permanent magnets are embedded in the rotor, and their magnetic force pulls back against the rotating field, so the rotor always lags the field by a fixed angle
At synchronous speed the stator current becomes zero and the motor is disconnected from the supply
At synchronous speed the rotor conductors do not cut the rotating field, so no current is induced and no torque is produced
power-electronics-035.explanation: An EMF is induced in the rotor conductors of an induction motor according to their speed relative to the rotating field, and a current flows. The force between this current and the field becomes the torque. If the rotor turned at the synchronous speed, the relative speed would be zero, so neither induced current nor torque would arise, and the rotor would slow down, unable to overcome the load and friction. An induction motor therefore turns slower than the synchronous speed by just enough (the slip) to produce the torque required.
choiceNotes: The rotor of a typical squirrel-cage induction motor has no permanent magnets. Synchronous motors are the ones that use permanent magnets.
Magnetizing current keeps flowing in the stator. Even at synchronous speed, the motor is not disconnected from the supply.
Correct. The slip lets current be induced in the rotor and produces torque.

power-electronics-036.question: When the speed of an induction motor is varied with an inverter, which of the following is the main reason the voltage-to-frequency ratio (V/f) is kept roughly constant?
choices: To keep the flux in the motor roughly constant and prevent magnetic saturation of the core or a lack of torque
Because keeping the voltage constant while lowering the frequency increases the flux and the torque, which makes the motor run faster
Because keeping the voltage-to-frequency ratio constant always makes the slip zero
power-electronics-036.explanation: The flux of an induction motor is roughly proportional to the applied voltage divided by the frequency. Lowering only the frequency while keeping the voltage increases the flux, saturates the core and draws a large magnetizing current. Lowering only the voltage, on the other hand, reduces the flux and makes torque hard to produce. For example, a 200 V, 50 Hz motor run at 25 Hz is supplied with about 100 V (V/f = 4 V/Hz). At low frequencies a torque boost, which raises the voltage slightly, compensates for the voltage drop across the winding resistance.
choiceNotes: Correct. Keeping V/f constant to maintain the flux is the idea behind V/f control.
The speed is set by the frequency. Lowering the frequency also lowers the synchronous speed.
Producing torque requires slip. Slip does not become zero under V/f control either.

power-electronics-037.question: A voltage of 24 V is applied to a DC motor with an armature resistance of 0.5 Ω and a back-EMF constant of 0.1 V/(rad/s), and the armature current is 8 A. Which of the following is the angular speed of rotation at this point?
choices: 40 rad/s
200 rad/s
240 rad/s
power-electronics-037.explanation: In a DC motor the applied voltage equals the voltage drop across the armature resistance plus the back EMF (V = R × I + E). The back EMF is E = 24 − 0.5 × 8 = 20 V, and from E = K_e × ω, ω = 20/0.1 = 200 rad/s (about 1910 min⁻¹). In SI units the torque constant has the same value as the back-EMF constant, so the torque is 0.1 × 8 = 0.8 N·m. When the load and therefore the current increase, the resistive drop increases and the back EMF decreases, so the motor slows slightly.
choiceNotes: This divides the resistive voltage drop (4 V) by the back-EMF constant.
This is the no-load angular speed, ignoring the resistive voltage drop.

power-electronics-038.question: Which of the following correctly describes a brushless DC motor?
choices: Brushes and a commutator switch the direction of the winding current mechanically, so no drive circuit such as an inverter is needed and it runs simply when connected to a DC supply
The rotor position is detected with sensors or other means, and an inverter switches the current in the stator windings electronically
It simply runs at the supply frequency when connected directly to an AC supply
power-electronics-038.explanation: In a brushed DC motor, the brushes and commutator mechanically switch the direction of the winding current as the motor turns. A brushless DC motor has permanent magnets on its rotor, and an inverter switches the current in the stator windings according to the rotor position (electronic commutation). The position is detected with sensors such as Hall elements or from the back EMF induced in the windings. With no brush wear or sparking, it is efficient and long-lived and is widely used in fans, drones, home appliances and cars.
choiceNotes: This describes a brushed DC motor. In a brushless DC motor, the drive circuit takes over switching the current.
Correct. Switching the current electronically eliminates the brushes and commutator.
Connecting directly to a supply and running at its frequency is how synchronous and induction motors are used. A brushless DC motor is run by a drive circuit.

power-electronics-039.question: Which of the following correctly combines what can happen when an induction motor driven by an inverter is decelerated quickly by lowering the frequency with the countermeasure?
choices: The rotor runs faster than the synchronous speed and acts as a generator, and the returning energy raises the DC voltage, so the energy is dissipated in a braking resistor or regenerated to the supply
During deceleration the motor current becomes zero and the motor is effectively disconnected from the supply, so nothing in particular happens and no countermeasure is needed
During deceleration the DC voltage of the inverter suddenly falls to zero, so the smoothing capacitor is removed to prevent voltage fluctuations from occurring at all
power-electronics-039.explanation: Lowering the frequency quickly lowers the synchronous speed, and the rotor, by inertia, turns faster than it, so the slip becomes negative and the induction motor acts as a generator. The generated energy returns to the DC side through the diodes of the inverter and charges the smoothing capacitor, raising the DC voltage. Too high a voltage destroys the devices, so a braking resistor is switched in to dissipate the energy as heat, or a regenerative converter returns the power to the supply. Trains and electric vehicles save energy with regenerative braking, which returns this energy to the overhead line or the battery.
choiceNotes: Correct. The deceleration energy returns to the DC side, so it has to be dealt with.
Current keeps flowing during deceleration, and energy returns from the motor to the inverter.
The DC voltage actually rises. The smoothing capacitor cannot be removed.

power-electronics-040.question: When an ideal transformer converts the primary voltage into a lower secondary voltage, which of the following correctly describes the relationship between the primary and secondary currents?
choices: The primary and secondary currents are always equal, regardless of the turns ratio
Lowering the voltage reduces the power by the same ratio, so the secondary current is also smaller than the primary current
Because the power is equal, reducing the voltage to 1/a makes the secondary current a times the primary current
power-electronics-040.explanation: An ideal transformer has no losses, so the power on the primary side equals the power on the secondary side (V1 × I1 = V2 × I2). The voltage is proportional to the number of turns (V1/V2 = N1/N2), and the current is inversely proportional to it (I1/I2 = N2/N1). For example, when a 10:1 turns ratio turns 100 V into 10 V and 5 A flows in the secondary, the primary current is 0.5 A. A transformer works by electromagnetic induction, so it can be used only with AC; converting DC requires first turning it into AC by switching.
choiceNotes: The current is inversely proportional to the number of turns. The currents are equal only when the turns ratio is 1:1.
Lowering the voltage makes the secondary current larger, so that the power is preserved.
Correct. The product of voltage and current (the power) is the same on the primary and secondary sides.
